transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-11
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Ortiz (Redwood AE), Sanjay Rao (Redwood SE), Tessa Nguyen (Redwood CSM); Priya Singh (Head of AI - Mariner), Greg Holloway (Security Architect), Lena Park (VP Eng), Omar Diaz (Platform Eng), Speaker 1 (temp)

Summary:
Quick intake focused on security posture required for a pilot: SOC2/ISO expectations, SSO/SAML integration, RBAC model, audit logs/retention, KMS/encryption options, and hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs. Mariner is leaning toward a pilot of Redwood Hosted but needs clarity on encryption-at-rest keys and audit retention to satisfy internal/compliance teams.

Topics: security artifacts, deployment options, KMS integration, retention windows, RBAC & SSO, audit logging granularity, canary/fallback for Dedicated/Private.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jamie Ortiz: ok hey everyone thanks for carving out time, uh this is Jamie from Redwood, along with Sanjay our solutions engineer and Tessa from success. how's everybody today?
[00:05] Priya Singh: good, thanks. we've been reviewing a few vendors this quarter, wanted to do a focused session just on security and retention stuff before we loop in procurement.
[00:12] Jamie Ortiz: perfect. high level goal for today's intake: understand your gating criteria for running inference on prod, whether hosted or private, and what artifacts you need to move forward.
[00:20] Greg Holloway: yeah, to be explicit: SOC two, ISO 27001 proof or roadmap, SSO with SAML, fine-grained RBAC, audit logs with at least 1 year retention, and KMS integration so we can manage keys. we also need to know data residency—where the logs and payloads are stored.
[00:35] Sanjay Rao: got it. quick note: when people say SOC two we sometimes transcribe as SOC too, sorry, but we have SOC 2 Type II artifacts and an ISO summary we can share. i'll flag the specific network diagrams and boundary docs you might want. are you planning to use Redwood-hosted initially or do you already have a mandate for VPC/on-prem?
[00:50] Lena Park: we prefer hosted for rapid testing, but legal/security have flagged key ownership as a blocker. they prefer customer-managed keys for any production data, especially for PII or claims data.
[01:00] Jamie Ortiz: totally expected. Redwood Hosted supports two main patterns: provider-managed encryption keys by default, and customer-managed KMS via our dedicated key provisioning for enterprise customers — we call that bring-your-own-KMS for Hosted, and in Private we can wire up your KMS directly in the VPC.
[01:15] Omar Diaz: when you say "wire up" the KMS in private, does that mean our HSM/KMS sits in our AWS account and Redwood's runtime calls it over a private peering?
[01:25] Sanjay Rao: yes, with Private deployment we establish VPC peering or PrivateLink, and the runtime communicates with your KMS endpoints in your account. you can require envelope encryption and we never persist plaintext keys. the only nuance is latency depending on where the KMS endpoint lives; small tradeoff.
[01:40] Speaker 1: (mumbled) latency's fine as long as it's under 120 ms median.
[01:45] Priya Singh: for initial pilot latency requirement is 150ms p50, but we will tighten for production. main blocker is the audit trail and retention controls, we need proof that we can capture request/response metadata and retain immutable logs for a year.
[01:58] Sanjay Rao: logs: we capture request metadata, model version, route, token counts, and operational alerts. for Hosted we store logs in our managed logging with retention options; we can export to customer S3 or to your SIEM via streaming for long-term retention. for Dedicated/Private you can route logs directly to your collectors in the VPC.
[02:18] Greg Holloway: so for Hosted export—are payloads included in the export? we are not comfortable with raw outputs leaving the system if they contain PHI.
[02:26] Jamie Ortiz: good callout. by default we redact sensitive fields from logs; full request/response payloads are considered high-sensitivity and only exported if you opt-in and we set up a secure ingestion to your collector. better pattern is to push request/response to a customer-owned S3 bucket with server-side encryption using your KMS.
[02:42] Lena Park: ok so that addresses key ownership and logs. next: SSO. we use Okta and require SAML 2.0 for RBAC. we also need SCIM for provisioning groups.
[02:52] Sanjay Rao: Redwood supports SAML SSO for console access and SCIM for provisioning. we map SAML assertions to RBAC roles. we can show you the claim mapping doc — sometimes claims are called 'role' vs 'groups' and mappings differ by IdP.
[03:06] Priya Singh: what about API keys? we want to avoid long-lived keys in workflows.
[03:11] Jamie Ortiz: we recommend short-lived tokens issued via our OIDC flow for service accounts; you can also integrate with your secret management to rotate keys. for Dedicated we can enforce IP allow lists and token lifetimes.
[03:22] Omar Diaz: is there audit trail for API key usage? we need to show who invoked a route and from which IP and service.
[03:28] Sanjay Rao: yes, each API request includes an attribution header with token owner, route, model, and we log IPs. logs feed into both our console and to your SIEM if you want.
[03:36] Speaker 1: (quiet) can you also tag requests by business unit?
[03:40] Jamie Ortiz: yes you can pass metadata in headers and we keep them in request metadata for observability; retention still obeys your retention policy. small caveat: customer metadata is not used for model training or telemetry unless you opt in.
[03:52] Priya Singh: important for compliance: we cannot have persistent model training on our data. does Redwood use customer data for model improvements?
[03:58] Jamie Ortiz: no, by default Redwood does not use customer payloads to train models. we have an opt-in program for aggregated telemetry but it's opt-in and subject to legal controls. we'll include that in the artifacts.
[04:10] Greg Holloway: can you walk me through an incident scenario? e.g., if an internal engineer accidentally opens a bucket with logs—what controls and detection are there?
[04:20] Sanjay Rao: detection: our platform emits alerts for unusual access patterns; Dedicated/Private you can forward logs to your SIEM and run normal SIEM playbooks. for Hosted we have SSO access history, admin action logs, and we can run an audit with timestamps. recovery: encrypted backups and immediate key rotation if a key compromise is suspected.
[04:37] Lena Park: do you provide SOC 2 reports on demand? our auditors ask for Type II evidence.
[04:42] Jamie Ortiz: yes, we can share SOC 2 Type II report under NDA. ISO 27001 summary and the certification status are in the pack we'll send.
[04:50] Priya Singh: retention windows—we were told you have default 90-day logs. we need 1-year immutable logs.
[04:57] Sanjay Rao: default is 90 for operational telemetry, but for compliance exports we support longer retention by routing to your S3 (you control lifecycle). for Hosted we can also extend retention to longer windows for an enterprise plan but export to a customer-owned store is the recommended durable option.
[05:10] Omar Diaz: PII masking — are you doing pattern redaction or schema-based scrubbing? we have structured payloads for claims, would prefer schema-based so we don't over-redact.
[05:19] Jamie Ortiz: we offer both. schema-based scrubbing (customer-provided schema) is the safer approach; sanjay can share the template for scrub rules. there are also regex-based rules for free text.
[05:28] Speaker 1: (interrupt) what's the uplift in latency with schema-based scrubbing?
[05:32] Sanjay Rao: typically negligible for short requests, maybe 5-15ms, but depends on request size. we can include sample numbers in the deep-dive.
[05:40] Priya Singh: okay next: RBAC. we need roles at team-level and route-level controls, e.g., only certain teams can call the payment-risk model. can Redwood do feature flags or route-based permissions?
[05:51] Sanjay Rao: yes, RBAC includes role -> route policies. in Dedicated/Private you can also enforce network policies. for Hosted we maintain role bindings in our IAM; you can integrate with SCIM and map groups to roles.
[06:03] Greg Holloway: retention of logs in the console—if a user has admin delete rights, can they delete audit logs?
[06:09] Tessa Nguyen: good question—by default audit logs are immutable for a window; admin actions are logged and we can restrict deletions in enterprise plans. for compliance we usually export to immutable storage you control.
[06:21] Priya Singh: about data residency—we have to ensure that logs and backups remain in the US East region. do you support region pinning?
[06:29] Jamie Ortiz: yes, we have region pinning for Hosted customers; for Private you can choose the region for the VPC. Dedicated gives predictable placement options. we'll include our regional footprint and how to pin resources.
[06:39] Lena Park: ok procurement will want pricing for a 6-month pilot — what's the typical pilot approach?
[06:44] Jamie Ortiz: usually a short Hosted pilot with customer-managed KMS and log export to S3 for 4-6 weeks, run a set of evaluation prompts, and then either roll to Dedicated or Private for higher control. we can also do a Dedicated reserved short-term for throughput testing if you need headroom.
[06:57] Priya Singh: we might run two parallel tests: a Hosted pilot to validate model outputs and an infra test for Private.
[07:03] Sanjay Rao: that works; for infra we usually do a capacity checklist and a smoke test to validate network, KMS latency, and metrics.
[07:10] Speaker 1: (background noise) sorry dropped for a second, can you repeat KMS latency impact?
[07:14] Sanjay Rao: yes: if KMS calls are in the critical token path (every request decrypts keys) you'd see extra latency. best practice is to use envelope keys with short-lived data keys in cache to minimize KMS round trips. in practice we've seen p50 latency impact of under 10-20ms when using envelope encryption correctly.
[07:34] Greg Holloway: do you support HSM-backed keys (cloud HSM or external HSM)?
[07:38] Jamie Ortiz: yes, we support cloud KMS including HSM-backed keys (AWS KMS with HSM, Google Cloud KMS), and for Private we can integrate with on-prem HSMs if network connectivity allows.
[07:48] Priya Singh: any red flags re: training data leakage — we need guaranteed separation between customer datasets and open models.
[07:55] Sanjay Rao: Redwood runtime isolates tenant data. hosted inference uses model binaries that are not retrained on customer payloads. we'll include an explicit statement for legal stating we don't persist user data for model training.
[08:06] Lena Park: what about pen tests and vulnerability scanning cadence? we need quarterly assessments and we run third-party pen tests too.
[08:12] Jamie Ortiz: we do regular vuln scans and annual pen tests; we can share the latest summary and point you to our SOC 2 controls that map to pen testing.
[08:21] Priya Singh: okay, last area: deletion/erasure. our policy says when a user requests deletion, logs/payloads must be deleted within 30 days across vendors. can you do that?
[08:33] Sanjay Rao: we support deletion requests; for Hosted we honor deletion requests and scrub records, but if data was exported to your customer-owned S3 that's under your control. for audit trails we can mark records as deleted and purge per agreed SLA. we'll map deletion flows in the doc.
[08:49] Speaker 1: (soft) is there a default SLA for deletion?
[08:52] Tessa Nguyen: standard is 30 days, enterprise can negotiate faster windows.
[08:56] Jamie Ortiz: great — i'll make sure deletion flows and evidence are in the package.
[09:00] Priya Singh: thanks—this was helpful. a few clarifying Qs: 1) how are model versions pinned for canaries; 2) do you keep KV cache in memory only or is some persisted; 3) does audit log include token-level cost breakdown?
[09:12] Sanjay Rao: quick answers: 1) you can pin model versions per route and use canary rollouts with traffic percentages. 2) KV cache is in-memory on the runtime; we persist snapshots only in Private if you opt-in for warm start. 3) logs include token counts and per-request cost estimate metadata.
[09:29] Greg Holloway: on canaries—if a canary fails do you have automatic fallback to a smaller model?
[09:33] Sanjay Rao: yes, we support automatic fallback policies to compatible model variants and can route by latency or cost constraints.
[09:39] Priya Singh: one last procurement note: we use standard MCN and DPAs — can Redwood sign our DPA?
[09:46] Jamie Ortiz: yes, we sign customer DPAs; legal will review terms. i'll include standard DPA and our data processing addendum.
[09:52] Omar Diaz: any documentation to share right after this call to make review faster?
[09:56] Jamie Ortiz: we'll send a security packet: SOC 2 Type II redacted report, ISO summary, network diagram, KMS patterns, SAML/SCIM configuration doc, logs export playbook, and the sample RBAC mapping.
[10:07] Priya Singh: perfect. thank you.
[10:09] Jamie Ortiz: recap and next steps: we share artifacts (SOC2/ISO/KMS patterns), schedule a Private deep-dive with Omar and Greg (Sanjay to lead), Mariner to send retention & PII inventory, and Tessa will schedule pilot kickoff.
[10:22] Lena Park: sounds good.
[10:25] Jamie Ortiz: ok we'll follow up via email. thanks everyone.
[10:28] Meeting end.

Notes on audio/transcription: occasional overlaps and a dropped line around 07:10-07:14; some names transcribed generically as 'Speaker 1'. Proper nouns like KMS or SOC 2 sometimes appear as K M S or SOC two in auto transcript.
